name: Johnny Cash
hook: A gospel singer whom Sun Records turned down until he came back with rockabilly, who played prisons and sang about Native American history, and whom Rick Rubin recorded alone with a guitar sixty years later.
blurb: Johnny Cash was born on 26 February 1932 in Kingsland, Arkansas, to a poor family of cotton farmers, and grew up singing gospel. In 1955 he auditioned at Sun Records in Memphis, the label that had just made Elvis Presley's first records. He sang mostly gospel, and the owner, Sam Phillips, told him Sun did not record gospel any more. A widely repeated story that Phillips told him to go and sin and come back with something he could sell was denied by Cash in 2002. Cash came back with his own songs, played with Luther Perkins and Marshall Grant, the Tennessee Two, in a chugging rhythm like a train. 'Hey, Porter' and 'Cry! Cry! Cry!' came out in June 1955, and 'Folsom Prison Blues' and 'I Walk the Line', which went to number one on the country chart, followed. He was at the Million Dollar Quartet session on 4 December 1956, and left for Columbia in 1958. In 1964 he made an album, 'Bitter Tears: Ballads of the American Indian', about the violent oppression of Native Americans. He played free concerts in prisons, and his live albums 'At Folsom Prison' (1968) and 'At San Quentin' (1969) went to number one on the country album chart. In 1994 the hip-hop and metal producer Rick Rubin signed him to American Recordings and recorded him alone in his living room, voice and acoustic guitar only, singing modern songs Rubin chose, and a new generation discovered him. The fourth album in the series, in 2002, included his cover of Nine Inch Nails' 'Hurt'. He died in Nashville on 12 September 2003.
